newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Surprise Venezuela TEM rate drop not seen as trend.
newsitem.headline: Surprise Venezuela TEM rate drop not seen as trend.

text.p: An unexpected recent slump in Venezuelan TEM yields may only be a temporary dip as the Central Bank is increasingly forced to raise interest rates in its fight against inflation, analysts said Friday.
"Although there's still a lot of liquidity in the system, it (the fall) surprised the market ... I'd expect the Bank to nudge up rates in the near future," said Santander economist Ricardo Penfold.

Yields on six-month TEM bills -- used as a benchmark for wider interest rates in the economy -- bucked an apparently rising trend to slump 123 basis points to 17.58 percent in the Central Bank's 60 billion bolivar ($125 million) Wednesday sale.
That drop was possible after a few major banks outbid other players in order to ensure placement in the TEM auction, analysts and traders said. Higher bond prices result in falling yields.
"This is clearly a positive from the Central Bank's perspective," wrote New York-based analysts group IDEA in a market commentary.
Lower yields allow the Central Bank to mop up excess liquidity in the domestic financial system without attracting international capital, IDEA said.
Lower rates, as well as spurring economic growth, also reduce Central Bank interest payments on an estimated 2.4 trillion bolivars ($4.9 billion) of outstanding TEMs.
But in the fine interplay between interest rate and foreign exchange rate policy, Wednesday's ploy is not always repeatable, analysts said.

Lower rates too far and the Central Bank prompts an abrupt investor flight into dollars, as happened at the end of February when six-month TEM yields fell to an historical 12.97 percent low and the bolivar momentarily plunged against the dollar.

And that hits the government's crucial inflation fight where it most hurts -- the strong bolivar, used in the near absence of other anti-inflation weapons, such as cuts in government spending, to bear down on prices.
So far the stable bolivar -- largely unchanged since currency controls were removed in April last year -- has given TEM investors a reasonable pick-up in dollar terms.

But in July the bolivar will have to begin slowly depreciating if it is not to break the floor of a foreign exchange band system that depreciates by 1.32 percent a month. The latest band was put in place in December and the bolivar has remained stoic.

Then the Central Bank may have to add higher interest rates to compensate for the still strong, but slowly depreciating, bolivar in its fight against inflation -- targeted at 30-35 percent after last year's 103 percent rate.
"The general feeling is of a slowly depreciating bolivar after July and higher interest rates," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Boris Molina said.
